q: Which command starts a service right now?
explain: `systemctl stop name` is the other half.

q: Which command makes a service start at every boot?
explain: `systemctl enable --now name` enables it and starts it at once.

q: How do you see whether a service runs, and its last lines of log?
explain: The first line says active (running), failed, or inactive (dead).

q: Where do you put a unit file you wrote?
explain: Packages use /usr/lib/systemd/system; yours takes precedence.

q: Why run a service as its own user (User=app) rather than root?
choices: If it gets hacked, the intruder only has that user's rights
explain: Least privilege. DynamicUser=yes even makes a throwaway user for it.

q: You just edited a unit file. What do you run before restarting it?
explain: Otherwise systemd keeps the version it read at boot.

q: How do you read one service's logs?
explain: Add -f to follow, -b for this boot only, -e to jump to the end.

q: Which command lists the units that failed?
explain: `systemctl list-units --type=service` shows them all.

q: What does `systemctl disable name` do?
choices: It stops it from starting at boot, without stopping it now
It stops it now and at boot
explain: `systemctl disable --now name` also stops it; `mask` makes it impossible to start.

q: Which command shows the unit file systemd actually uses?
explain: It prints the file and every drop-in override on top of it.

q: In a .service file, which section holds ExecStart?
explain: [Unit] describes and orders it, [Install] says where `enable` hooks it.

q: What does WantedBy=multi-user.target in [Install] mean?
choices: `enable` links it into the normal boot
It only runs for logged-in users
It waits for a graphical session
explain: multi-user.target is the usual server boot; graphical.target pulls it in too.

q: Your program stays in the foreground. Which Type fits?
explain: Type=forking is for daemons that fork and exit; systemd then needs PIDFile.

q: A script runs once and exits, but the unit should count as done. What do you write?
explain: That is how one-off setup units (mounts, firewall rules) are written.

q: What does Restart=on-failure do?
choices: It restarts the service only when it exits with an error
It restarts it every time it stops
It restarts it once a day
It restarts it when the machine boots
explain: RestartSec= spaces the attempts; StartLimitBurst= stops endless loops.

q: After=network-online.target alone is not enough. Why?
choices: After= only orders; Wants= is what pulls the target in
The target does not exist by default
After= needs a number of seconds
explain: Write Wants=network-online.target and After=network-online.target together.

q: Where should a service's database password go?
choices: A root-only file: EnvironmentFile= or LoadCredential=
explain: Unit files are readable by all and `systemctl show` prints Environment=; ExecStart arguments show in ps.

q: Which command checks a unit file for mistakes before you use it?
explain: `man 5 systemd.service` lists every option, with examples.

q: What is a drop-in override?
choices: A .conf in /etc/systemd/system/name.d/, changing a few lines
A copy of the unit in your home
A unit that replaces another at boot
A comment block at the end of the unit
explain: `systemctl edit name` creates it, so a package update keeps your change.

q: What replaces a cron job in systemd?
choices: A .timer unit with OnCalendar=, enabled like a service
explain: `systemctl list-timers` shows the next runs; the timer starts the service of the same name.
